Sorry I've forgotten to share the code (using the scales package) :

<<echo=FALSE>>=
  nsims <- 150
@
  \begin{figure}[t]
<<gaussian, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=6, out.width='.9\\linewidth', fig.show='animate', tidy=FALSE, crop=TRUE, dev='tikz'>>=
layout(matrix(c(1,1,2,3), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE))
  for (i in 1:nsims) {
    set.seed(666)
    simulation <- rnorm(i)
    #
    cexpoints <- rep(1,i)
    cexpoints[i] <- 1.8
    cols <- alpha(rep("red", i), 0.5)
    cols[i] <- alpha("red",1)
    #
    ats <- seq(-4,4,by=2)
    labs <- c("", "$\\mu-2\\sigma$","$\\mu$","$\\mu+2\\sigma$",  "")
        plot(1:nsims, rep(0,nsims), type="n", ylim=c(-4,4), axes=FALSE, 
         xlab="observation", ylab=NA)
    axis(1)
    axis(2, at=ats, labels=labs)
    grid(nx=NA,ny=NULL)
    points(1:i, simulation, col=cols, cex=cexpoints, pch=19)
    #
    curve(dnorm(x), from=-4, to=4, axes=FALSE, xlab=NA, ylab=NA, lwd=3, col="blue", 
          main="Simulations")
    labs <- c(expression(mu-4~sigma), expression(mu-2~sigma), expression(mu),  expression(mu+2~sigma),  expression(mu+4~sigma))
    axis(1, at=seq(-4,4,by=2), labels=paste0("$", seq(-4,4,by=2), "\\sigma$"))
    points(x=simulation, y=rep(0,i), col=cols, pch=19, cex=cexpoints)
    #
    hist(simulation, breaks=seq(-4,4,by=1), ylim=c(0,1), freq=FALSE, axes=FALSE, 
        ylab="Proportion", xlab=NA, 
         main="Histogram")
    axis(1, at=seq(-4,4,by=2), labels=c("$\\mu-4\\sigma$","$\\mu-2\\sigma$","$\\mu$","$\\mu+2\\sigma$", "$\\mu+4\\sigma$"))
    ats <- seq(0,1,by=0.25)
    axis(2, at=ats, labels=paste0("$", 100*ats, "\\%$"))
    curve(dnorm(x), add=TRUE, col="blue", lwd=2, lty="dashed")
    #
    #
  }
@
  \end{figure}

messages.subject: Re: layout() with tikz device and animate show
parts:
Better like this: https://www.dropbox.com/s/prmqkpk92ks8s2e/gaussian_anim_solo.pdf
I'll try to write an article about LaTeX animations (with and without knitr) on my blog in the near future. By the way, is it possible to embed such a pdf animation in a html page, with available controls and without requiring to open the pdf with Acrobat ?

My code is below. I would be glad if anybody had any comment about possible enhancements (about quality rendering, or good practices in general).


\documentclass{beamer}

\mode<presentation> {
  \usetheme{Boadilla}
}

\usepackage[buttonsize=1em]{animate} 
\usepackage{helvet} % fonts package
\usepackage{graphicx} % Allows including images

\begin{document}

<<setup, echo=FALSE>>=
library(scales)
# polyCurve() allows to shade an area below a curve:
polyCurve <- function(x, y, from, to, n = 50, miny,
                      col = "red", border = col) {
  drawPoly <- function(fun, from, to, n = 50, miny, col, border) {
    Sq <- seq(from = from, to = to, length = n)
    polygon(x = c(Sq[1], Sq, Sq[n]),
            y = c(miny, fun(Sq), miny),
            col = col, border = border)
  }
  lf <- length(from)
  stopifnot(identical(lf, length(to)))
  if(length(col) != lf)
    col <- rep(col, length.out = lf)
  if(length(border) != lf)
    border <- rep(border, length.out = lf)
  if(missing(miny))
    miny <- min(y)
  interp <- approxfun(x = x, y = y)
  mapply(drawPoly, from = from, to = to, col = col, border = border,
         MoreArgs = list(fun = interp, n = n, miny = miny))
  invisible()
}
@


\begin{frame}
\frametitle{The Gaussian sampler}

  % initialisiation :
<<gaussian_anim_params, echo=FALSE>>=
  nsims <- 100
  eps <- .1
  xx <- seq(-4,4,length=150)
  yy <- dnorm(xx)
  rgba <- col2rgb("gray")
  tgray <- rgb(rgba[1,1], rgba[2,1], rgba[3,1], alpha=95, maxColorValue=255)
@

  \begin{figure}
<<gaussian_anim, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=6, out.width='.9\\linewidth', fig.show='animate', tidy=FALSE, crop=TRUE, dev='tikz', aniopts='controls'>>=
layout(matrix(c(1,1,2,3), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE))
  for (i in 1:nsims) {
    set.seed(666)
    simulation <- rnorm(i)
    #
    cexpoints <- rep(1,i)
    cexpoints[i] <- 1.8
    cols <- alpha(rep("red", i), 0.5)
    cols[i] <- alpha("red",1)
    #
    par(mar=c(2,5,2,2))
    ats <- seq(-4,4,by=2)
    labs <- c("$\\mu-4\\sigma$", "$\\mu-2\\sigma$","$\\mu$","$\\mu+2\\sigma$",  "$\\mu+4\\sigma$")
    plot(1:nsims, rep(0,nsims), type="n", ylim=c(-4,4), axes=FALSE, 
         xlab="observation", ylab=NA)
    rect(1-eps, -2, nsims+eps, 2, 
     col=tgray,
     border="transparent")
    axis(1)
    axis(2, las=2, at=ats, labels=labs)
    grid(nx=NA,ny=NULL)
    points(1:i, simulation, col=cols, cex=cexpoints, pch=19)
    abline(h=0, col="blue", lty="dotted")
    #
    plot(xx, yy, type = "l", lwd=4, col="blue", xlim=c(-4,4), 
               panel.first =
                 polyCurve(xx, yy, from = -2, to = 2,
                           col = tgray, border = tgray), 
      ylab=NA, xlab=NA, 
      axes=FALSE, 
      main="Simulations")
    axis(1, at=seq(-4,4,by=2), labels=c("$\\mu-4\\sigma$","$\\mu-2\\sigma$","$\\mu$","$\\mu+2\\sigma$", "$\\mu+4\\sigma$"))
    points(x=simulation, y=rep(0,i), col=cols, pch=19, cex=cexpoints)
    #
    n <- i
    hstep <- 1
    hist(simulation, breaks=seq(-4,4,by=hstep), ylim=c(0,n*1.02), freq=TRUE, axes=FALSE, 
         ylab="Proportion", xlab=NA, 
         main="Histogram")
    axis(1, at=seq(-4,4,by=2), labels=c("$\\mu-4\\sigma$","$\\mu-2\\sigma$","$\\mu$","$\\mu+2\\sigma$", "$\\mu+4\\sigma$"))
    numlabs <- seq(0,1,by=0.25)
    labs <- paste0("$", 100*numlabs, "\\%$")
    ats <- n*numlabs
    axis(2, las=2, at=ats, labels=labs, cex.axis=0.85, hadj=0.9)
    curve(n*dnorm(x), add=TRUE, col="blue", lwd=2, lty="dashed")
    #
  }
@
  \end{figure}

\end{frame}

\end{document}

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: layout() with tikz device and animate show
parts:
That is possible, but not straightfoward. It requires very good
understanding of knitr (I do not want to promote it, but the knitr
book will be helpful). Two key steps are:

1. convert tikz/PDF to PNG; you can use ImageMagick/convert for this
2. embed images in HTML; use knitr::hook_scianimator() as the
animation function instead of the default hook_ffmpeg_html()

You can see plenty of examples at http://vis.supstat.com/ which were
generated from knitr, but I do not have time to describe everything in
this reply; the website is open source on Github, so you can probably
figure it out by yourself.

Regards,
Yihui
